title: Predestination
hook: Calvin and the Reformed stress God's sovereign choosing; they find comfort in it

segments.voice: Yesterday, Augustine and Pelagius: can we be good without grace? Your line was grace first. Did you pause before your one task? Day one thousand seventy-eight.

What is your only comfort in life and in death? That's the first question of the Heidelberg Catechism, a teaching book of the Reformed churches. Children in some Reformed congregations learn it by heart. The answer, put simply, is this: that I am not my own, but belong, body and soul, to my faithful Savior Jesus Christ. Notice the word at the heart of the question. Comfort. Not argument, not fear. Today's word is one that some people hear as cold, even frightening. The people who hold it closest speak of it as comfort. Today: predestination.
screen: `YOUR ONLY COMFORT IN LIFE AND DEATH?`
`A COLD WORD, OR A WARM ONE?`

segments.voice: The word is in the Bible. Paul writes in Romans, in the King James: "For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son." And in Ephesians: "he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world." Yesterday, Augustine said grace must come first. John Calvin and the Reformed churches after him followed that line all the way back. If grace comes first, they said, then before any of us chose God, God chose us. Salvation rests on God's choosing, not on our deciding well. They call this God's sovereignty: God is God, and God's purposes don't fail. And here is where the warmth comes in. Reformed Christians speak of this as comfort. If my hold on God depended on me, they say, it would be as shaky as I am on a bad day. But if it depends on God's choosing, it's as steady as God. Jesus says of his sheep, in John's Gospel: "neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand." That's the picture: not a ladder you have to keep climbing, but a hand that won't let go. The doctrine raises hard questions, and Reformed teachers admit it: what about those not chosen? Some of them answer with humility, and leave the question with God. Other Christians answer the question differently, and tomorrow we'll hear them. Look back at this week: a dance, a world from nothing, a fossil, an image, a wound, a long argument about grace, and now a hand. Seven ways of asking who God is, and who we are.

Here's the practice: rest in being held. Sit back so the chair takes your whole weight. Let your shoulders drop. Feel the floor under your feet doing its job without any help from you. For a minute, stop holding yourself up. Notice how much effort you usually spend just keeping yourself together. Then set some of it down. If you pray, you can rest in the line from John: neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand. If you don't, just let the chair and the floor hold you, and let that be enough for now. The bell holds the time.
Predestination. God choosing before we choose. Calvin and the Reformed churches stress it, and they speak of it as a comfort: held by a hand that won't let go.
Your line: held by his choosing. Today, the next time you catch yourself gripping something tight, a plan, a worry, a phone, loosen your hand for one breath. Day one thousand seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Reformed and Presbyterian churches teach predestination in their confessions and catechisms, and some members learn the Heidelberg Catechism's first question and answer, on comfort in life and death, by heart.

fork.setup: a Reformed friend tells you predestination is their deepest comfort. you ask why. what do they say?
options: because it means they can stop caring how they live.
because their hold on God rests on God's choosing, not their own steadiness.
because they know exactly who is chosen.
fork.reveal: Reformed Christians say that if salvation depended on them, it would be as shaky as they are. resting on God's choosing, it's as steady as God.

original.note: Greek: to mark out beforehand. Paul's word in Romans 8:29, predestinate in the King James.
